source.title: FIRE: Flexible Integration of Data Quality Ratings for Effective Pretraining
source.authors: Liangyu Xu; Xuemiao Zhang; Fei-Yu Duan; Sirui Wang; Rong-Xiang Weng; Jin-Gang Wang; Xun-Liang Cai

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream accuracy as pretraining tokens vary, which bears on V6, but it does not fit or test the original held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The authors cite scaling laws as motivation but do not measure held-out loss, parameter-count scaling, compute-optimal allocations, or extrapolation. Main-results tables compare data-selection methods at fixed training settings, so those comparisons are not rows for the claim. Figure 4 reports downstream accuracy curves over pretraining tokens; the text gives qualitative comparisons but not numerical curve values.
record.test_reason: This is a data-selection method paper. It cites Kaplan et al. (2020) only as motivation. It fits no scaling law and reports no held-out loss. It does not compare model sizes to test predictability. The Figure 4 token sweeps compare FIRE against Random selection for one 1.3B model, with no numbers given and no claim of predictable scaling. The downstream results are evidence about the method's own performance, not about whether downstream accuracy tracks scale or loss predictably.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that FIRE, which integrates multiple aligned quality raters with orthogonality weighting and progressive selection, outperforms other selection methods. They say it raises average downstream accuracy (by 2.9% over Random) with under 37.5% of Random's data. The HellaSwag caveat appears only in the analysis section, not the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates quality-based pretraining data selection, not the original loss-scaling measurement or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream results vary by task: the text describes consistent FIRE advantages on ARC-E, ARC-C, and SciQ, but not on HellaSwag.

fits_no_version.finding: Quality-rated data selection (FIRE) reaches Random's target downstream accuracy with under 37.5% of the tokens for a 1.3B model. It also beats Random by 1.6% average for a 3B model trained on 200B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data quality selection shifts the data-efficiency of downstream accuracy relative to random selection, at a fixed model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The token-sweep results are shown in plots without numerical values in the text; only one model size is used for the token-varying comparison, and no pretraining-loss or scaling-law fits are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows from the fixed-setting method comparisons in Tables 1 and 2: they compare data-selection approaches rather than report downstream performance as scale varies. No separate FIRE Progressive rows were extracted because the text does not give task-specific qualitative outcomes for its token-sweep curves.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no fits and no extrapolation.
All: no shape variation at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modalities or regimes fitted.
All: no test of predictable downstream improvement with scale or loss. Token curves are shown only as method comparisons, with no values.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link conflated the method-versus-baseline accuracy curves with a test of downstream scaling predictability. Table 2 compares 1.3B and 3B models, but only as a method comparison at different budgets. It does not test scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study varies pretraining tokens for one model size and reports downstream accuracy, but does not test power-law predictability, relate performance to pretraining loss, or test variation in model scale.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
